name: Data health
description: Does the pipeline still deliver what the contract promises? Every card cites a KPI id from docs/kpi_definitions.md. Source: the gold marts in the one Postgres (database 'marts', schema 'marts').

cards.name: KPI-01 · trips ingested, all months
cards.sql: SELECT SUM(kpi_01_trips_ingested) AS trips_ingested FROM marts.monthly_kpis

visualization_settings.card.description: KPI-01 summed over every ingested month — the row count AFTER the contract, not before.

cards.name: KPI-01 · months in the mart
cards.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS months_ingested FROM marts.monthly_kpis

visualization_settings.card.description: Freshness, asked as coverage: a catalogue pointing at five months of eight answers every query happily, just smaller.

cards.name: KPI-01 · newest month ingested
cards.sql: SELECT MAX(month) AS newest_month FROM marts.monthly_kpis

visualization_settings.card.description: Freshness. A board that cannot say how old its newest data is cannot be seen to go stale.

cards.name: KPI-02 · overall rejection rate
cards.sql: SELECT ROUND((100.0 * SUM(rows_rejected) / NULLIF(SUM(rows_in), 0))::numeric, 4) AS rejection_rate_pct FROM marts.monthly_kpis

visualization_settings.card.description: KPI-02 over all months. The single number is the headline; the series beside it is the story (it rises monotonically).

cards.name: KPI-01 · trips ingested per month
cards.sql: SELECT month, split, kpi_01_trips_ingested AS trips_ingested FROM marts.monthly_kpis ORDER BY month

visualization_settings.card.description: KPI-01 by month. Read with KPI-02: a fall here with a flat rejection rate is a quieter month; a fall with a rising rate is a quality problem.

cards.name: KPI-02 · rejection rate SERIES, by month
cards.sql: SELECT month, kpi_02_rejection_rate_pct AS rejection_rate_pct, rows_in, rows_rejected FROM marts.monthly_kpis ORDER BY month

visualization_settings.card.description: A SERIES, not a number, on purpose: the observed 2019 rate rises monotonically 1.428% -> 2.020%, and the ingest guard (10% refusal) sees none of that. A single average would hide the trend that matters.

cards.name: KPI-03 · rejections attributed per rule (every rule, including the zeroes)
cards.sql: SELECT rule, SUM(rejected_by) AS rejected_by, SUM(matched) AS matched, COUNT(*) AS months_present FROM marts.rejections_by_rule GROUP BY rule ORDER BY rejected_by DESC, rule

visualization_settings.card.description: KPI-03. The permanently-zero rules are rendered deliberately: a rule you cannot see cannot be seen to START firing. 'rejected_by' attributes each dropped row to exactly one rule; 'matched' counts every rule a row tripped.

cards.name: KPI-03 · rejections per rule, by month
cards.sql: SELECT month, rule, rejected_by FROM marts.rejections_by_rule ORDER BY month, rule

visualization_settings.card.description: KPI-03 over time — which rule is driving KPI-02's rise.

cards.name: KPI-04 · undocumented-value rate (drift by VALUE)
cards.sql: SELECT month, kpi_04_undocumented_pct AS undocumented_pct, kpi_04_undocumented_rows AS undocumented_rows FROM marts.monthly_kpis ORDER BY month

visualization_settings.card.description: KPI-04: rows carrying a value the TLC dictionary does not describe (VendorID 4/5, payment_type 0, RatecodeID 99). Drift by VALUE is the quieter sibling of drift by column (gotcha #31). Observed 2019: falls monotonically 1.3778% -> 0.5616% while KPI-02 rises.

cards.name: KPI-05 · raw-byte provenance (sha256 per month)
cards.sql: SELECT month, split, raw_file, raw_bytes, kpi_05_raw_sha256 AS raw_sha256 FROM marts.monthly_kpis ORDER BY month

visualization_settings.card.description: KPI-05. The manifest is timestamp-free by design: a diff here means the BYTES moved, not that a file was touched. TLC backfills (gotcha #6), so this is the card that notices.
